lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah say goodbye, and look back
lead.head: The flow stops, the stock stays

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 128

body: “For the last time, I’m Amit and this is Ajay.” With that, Amit Varma opened the final episode of *Everything is Everything*, the weekly show he and Ajay Shah have made for two and a half years.
Neither host wanted to stop, Varma said. Each had rea­sons, and when the two talked, the rea­sons co­in­cided. “All good things come to an end,” he said. “Better things lie ahead of both of us.”

Shah’s main rea­son was that he had said what he wanted to say. A life­time of hik­ing gives one episode, a life­time of cy­cling an­other, a life­time of poker an­other. “One can’t live more lives and cre­ate these bod­ies of knowl­edge,” he said. {128-S01}

As the show moved away from that life­time ma­te­rial, the episodes grew harder and costlier to make. Shah is also writ­ing a book on taxes with Vijay Kelkar and Arvind Modi, and has three con­fer­ences to run in early December.

Varma’s rea­son was band­width. The show came out every Friday at 12 o’clock, he said, even when he was in hos­pi­tal and when Shah broke his leg. But he also pro­duced it, and it was on his mind all the time. {128-S02}
He wants to write, and to take a pause. “On our own, we would not have stopped the show,” he said.
## A sin­gle pic­ture
Looking back, Shah said he was “truly happy and proud”. He wanted to claim some­thing for the show.
India, he said, is a coun­try where statism is all-pervasive. Attempts to reimag­ine it have been piece­meal, and a piece­meal re­form fails when ev­ery­thing around it is dis­torted by the state.
The show, he ar­gued, of­fers a com­plete pic­ture in­stead, with peo­ple, free­dom, con­sent and agency at the heart of the story. {128-C01}
Taken to­gether, he said, the episodes an­swer “this big­gest of all sto­ries”: why India is poor, and why its cap­i­tal and labour are not mo­bilised into high-quality firms. {128-C02}

Varma de­scribed it dif­fer­ently. The show, he said, “fused pub­lic pur­pose with pri­vate pas­sion”: along­side the state, firms and fi­nance sat read­ing, chess, cricket, poker and sto­ries that should be films.
## Seven lessons
Shah then asked for the higher-order lessons. Varma, who said the show had shaped him, gave seven, ad­dressed to cre­ators.

Have a bias for ac­tion. Don’t let per­fec­tion get in the way of pro­duc­tion. Be loved by a few rather than liked by many. Be au­then­tic. Build com­mu­nity. Use the free­dom that comes from own­ing the means of pro­duc­tion. Play the long game.

Running through them was the economist’s dis­tinc­tion be­tween stock and flow. A book is stock: it out­lives its au­thor. A weekly show is flow, to be thought aloud and put out. But over time, Varma said, a body of flow be­comes stock.
The episodes, he said, re­main out there for ev­ery­one to watch. In that sense, the show isn’t over.
## Not quite the end
Shah would not call it an end. “Everything that dies, some day it comes back,” he said, urg­ing Varma to res­ur­rect the show in some form. {128-J07}
Varma does want to do more on YouTube one day, but not under this name. *Everything is Everything*, he said, is the two of them.
“The journey’s been great,” he said. “So thank you Ajay for com­ing on our jour­ney with me.”
“Thank you, Amit,” Shah replied, “for bring­ing me to this jour­ney.”

second.label: The co-host question
second.head: No understudy for Ajay
second.deck: Amit Varma on why the show will not carry on with someone else

pic.caption: Amit Varma (right) on why there will be no new co-host, with Ajay Shah

body: Ajay Shah urged Amit Varma to res­ur­rect the show: the ethos, the peo­ple and the au­di­ence were all still there. Others sug­gested Varma carry on with a new co-host. {128-S07}

The first name that came to mind was Pranay Kotasthane, whom both hosts deeply ad­mire. Varma talked to him, and Kotasthane’s view, which Varma shares, was that the show was its two hosts and no­body else.

Varma and Kotasthane may make a sep­a­rate, fun show one day, with Bollywood and Hindi in it. Under this name, it would feel odd. Varma al­ways meant the chan­nel to carry sev­eral shows. For this one, he said, “the jour­ney is done”. {#journeydone}

quote.text: Everything is Everything is you and me. People as­so­ciate it with us.

third.head: Two years, no peeking

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the two-year pact

body: When the show began, Amit Varma sat Ajay Shah down and pro­posed a deal: they would make it for two years with­out look­ing at the num­bers. “Now this man did not obey me,” Varma said. “He kept look­ing at the an­a­lyt­ics.” {128-S05}
The idea came from Ali Abdaal, who once said that any­one start­ing a YouTube chan­nel should not look at the num­bers for two years. {#abdaal}

Varma’s rea­son­ing was that the mo­ment out­side ap­plause mat­ters, you start dumb­ing your­self down and drift from the au­then­tic­ity that makes you spe­cial. Validation never comes early any­way, he said, “be­cause you will suck at the start”.
Shah came a long way re­gard­less. “When we started, you were so awk­ward and clumsy,” Varma said. “Today you’re a con­sum­mate pro­fes­sional.”

box.title: Threads to pull
box.text: Amit Varma sees the show as one long con­ver­sa­tion with threads you can pull: Episodes 25 and 26 and the pub­lic choice episode on the state, the episodes on firms, *The Beauty of Finance*, and the episode on ed­u­ca­tion. {#state}

sections.label: The reasons
sections.head: Said what he had to say
sections.caption: one lifetime of knowledge
body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah each had rea­sons to end the show, and when they talked, they found the rea­sons co­in­cided. Shah had two: “one big rea­son” and “a less big rea­son”.
The big one was that nice, com­plete episodes come out of life­times of knowl­edge, and there are not many of them. Shah has one life­time, he said, and he had said what he wanted to say. {128-S01}

The less big one was cost. As the con­ver­sa­tion moved away from fa­mil­iar life­time ma­te­rial, the work grew harder. He is writ­ing a book on taxes with Vijay Kelkar and Arvind Modi, and runs three con­fer­ences in early December. “It is just a gru­elling pace,” he said. {#conferences}

Varma had hoped for a dif­fer­ent list. “When you said so many, I was hop­ing you’re gonna say so many books,” he said; he has been urg­ing Shah to write sev­eral, among them *Invisible Infrastructure*. {128-J01}
## Bandwidth, not lo­gis­tics

Varma’s own rea­son was men­tal space. Shooting took three days every six weeks. Producing, which he also did, meant build­ing the list of on-screen in­serts for each episode and talk­ing over the edit every day. “It was tak­ing up mind space,” he said.
He loves the show and would not have stopped on his own, but he wants to write.
~ Varma would rather end on a note where they can look back with hap­pi­ness. “No man steps in the same river twice,” he said. {128-J06}

quote.text: I have one life­time of knowl­edge. I have only one life­time of knowl­edge.

art.caption: Amit Varma on one lifetime of knowledge

sections.label: The body of work
sections.head: Solow’s model, opened up
sections.caption: the Solow model
body: Ajay Shah wanted to “claim some­thing im­por­tant”. India, he said, is a coun­try where statism is all-pervasive and “more and more state co­er­cion” is the de­fault an­swer to ev­ery­thing.

Efforts to reimag­ine the coun­try have been piece­meal, and no sin­gle re­form works when ev­ery­thing around it is dis­torted by the state. The show, Shah ar­gued, of­fers a com­plete pic­ture, with peo­ple, free­dom, con­sent and agency at its heart. The state is needed, “but it’s not the essence”. {128-C01}
## Three black boxes
Then he went “one step big­ger”. The crude Solow model makes out­put a func­tion of labour, cap­i­tal and one magic num­ber, pro­duc­tiv­ity. After in­de­pen­dence, peo­ple read it causally.

Every term, Shah said, hides a deeper story. India’s em­ploy­ment rate is some­thing like 36 or 38 per cent of peo­ple aged 16 to 64. {#employment} In China the ratio is dou­ble. The prob­lem is not a short­age of peo­ple but that firms are not form­ing to put them to work.

There is in­fi­nite cap­i­tal in the world econ­omy, yet India has not opened its cap­i­tal ac­count to bring down the cost of cap­i­tal. Low pro­duc­tiv­ity comes from a thou­sand in­sti­tu­tional fail­ures to cre­ate checks and bal­ances and cre­ative de­struc­tion. {128-C02}
~ Amit Varma’s gloss was that the show had fused pub­lic pur­pose with pri­vate pas­sion, the pol­icy be­side read­ing, chess, cricket and poker. {128-C03}

quote.text: We’ve told this big­gest of all sto­ries that why is India poor?

portraits.credit: Olaf Storbeck from Düsseldorf, Deutschland, CC BY-SA 2.0

sections.label: The first lessons
sections.head: Done is the road to right
sections.caption: stock and flow
body: The show taught Amit Varma noth­ing rad­i­cally new, he said, but hard­ened ideas he held vaguely. The first: have a bias for ac­tion.

He called it “a dan­ger­ous phrase”: Ajay Shah has often ar­gued that the state, whose every act is deeply con­se­quen­tial, should move grad­u­ally. {128-C04} For cre­ators, though, “bias for ac­tion is good, go for it.”

The sec­ond les­son came from their friend Vinay Sitapati: “Don’t let per­fec­tion get in the way of pro­duc­tion.” {128-J09} Every episode has some­thing wrong with it, Varma ad­mit­ted, and he still cringes at his own footage.
## Stock and flow

A re­lated frame came from eco­nom­ics. Stock is like wealth: it stays. Flow is like in­come: it keeps com­ing. For a cre­ator, books are stock, such as *In Service of the Republic* and Shah’s forth­com­ing book on tax­a­tion. Columns, blog posts, news­let­ters and weekly shows are flow. {128-C06}

Varma took an image from Philip Larkin’s poem *This Be the Verse*, in which mis­ery “deep­ens like a coastal shelf”. Knowledge is a coastal shelf too, he said, and stock goes into its lay­ers. {128-R17}
~ So ag­o­nise over a book, he said, but with flow, think aloud and put it out. Doing so makes you a bet­ter thinker, and the feed­back finds holes in your ar­gu­ment.

quote.text: In fact, get­ting it done is the path to get­ting it right. Production is a path to per­fec­tion.

sections.label: Three, four, five
sections.head: Better loved than liked
sections.caption: being loved by a few
body: Amit Varma’s third les­son was a line from Paul Graham, who used it of star­tups: it is bet­ter to be loved by a few than liked by many. {128-R19}

Fewer num­bers bring deeper en­gage­ment, Varma said. Every time he goes to Blossom’s book­store in Bangalore, two peo­ple come up to him. {#blossoms} The show’s com­ment sec­tion, he re­ported with pride, is won­der­ful, and he has met three or four peo­ple through their com­ments.
Chasing what­ever is trend­ing, by con­trast, is “a path to medi­ocrity”, be­cause ev­ery­body is chas­ing it. {128-C07}
## Just be your­self
The fourth les­son: “It is both easy and re­ward­ing to be au­then­tic.” Over a long run, Varma said, any pre­tence pro­duces con­trived con­tent that oth­ers see through. {128-C08}
Being your­self, he added, is the only thing that sets you apart from “the other eight bil­lion peo­ple on this planet”.

The fifth les­son was com­mu­nity, the only thing, Varma said, that a cre­ator can mon­e­tise. {128-C09} Readers al­ready pay with their time and at­ten­tion, even when an ar­ti­cle is free: “My time is worth money.” The pub­lisher and the ad­ver­tiser, the two mid­dle­men of the old model, are going away.
~ Yet the hosts never both­ered to mon­e­tise their com­mu­nity, he said, “be­cause that’s not the point”.

quote.text: If you are a cre­ator and you want to mon­e­tise, you can only mon­e­tise the com­mu­nity, the peo­ple who re­ally care about you.

art.caption: Amit Varma on being loved by a few

sections.label: The last lessons
sections.head: No gatekeeper required
sections.caption: the freedom of form
body: Amit Varma’s sixth les­son was free­dom. Take a show like this one to main­stream media, he said, and they would laugh the hosts out of the room: in­fla­tion tar­get­ing, the bank­ruptcy code, and two hosts who “aren’t even like glam­orous, amaz­ing peo­ple”.
*The Seen and the Unseen*, with its ten-hour con­ver­sa­tions with econ­o­mists, would have fared no bet­ter. {128-J04}

But cre­ators now have the means of pro­duc­tion at hand, Varma said. There is no gate­keeper, and form is free: one hour, 90 min­utes, two hours, or one con­ver­sa­tion split into two episodes. {128-C10} “Creative”, he added, cov­ers ed­u­ca­tors and so­cial-sector thinkers as much as writ­ers and film­mak­ers.
## The long game

The sev­enth les­son was to play the long game, which Varma called a les­son in pub­lic pol­icy too. {#longgame} Forget whether the light­ing is good or what your friends will say, he said, and be in­ter­nally driven.

The mo­ment out­side ap­plause mat­ters, he ar­gued, you start dumb­ing your­self down. And early ap­plause never comes, be­cause ev­ery­one is bad at the start. You get bet­ter only by con­stant it­er­a­tion.
~ In that sense, he said, the show is not over: “these episodes are still out there for you for ev­ery­one to watch.”

quote.text: We didn’t have to go through a gate­keeper, we had the means of pro­duc­tion at our hands, we didn’t have to worry about form.

art.caption: Amit Varma (right) on the freedom of form, with Ajay Shah

quote.text: Build that body of work. It is a repos­i­tory. And in a sense, it is flow be­com­ing stock. Build that body of work, play the long game.

p3.title: The stories they told
p3.deck: Four tales from the farewell, and what each one says about making things

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the deadline he never missed
stories.head: Twelve o’clock, come what may
body: Amit Varma de­scribes him­self as “re­ally bloody minded” about see­ing things through once they start. *The Seen and the Unseen* ran weekly for seven years and is now fort­nightly, and he has never missed a sched­uled re­lease. {#sevenyears}

*Everything is Everything* kept the same dis­ci­pline: every Friday at 12 o’clock, an episode came out. Once, very early on, it slipped to a Saturday. Otherwise it held, “even when I was in hos­pi­tal get­ting a pro­ce­dure done or Ajay broke his leg”. {128-S02}
The shoot­ing, Varma said, was not a big deal. Once every six weeks the hosts gath­ered at a friend’s farm­house and, over three days, shot six episodes, two a day. {#farmhouse}

The bur­den lay else­where. Varma also pro­duced the show. When the ed­i­tor, Nomsita MS Haritashya, sent him a rough cut, he drew up the painstak­ingly de­tailed list of in­serts that ap­pear on screen. Then the two of them talked over the edit every day until the episode went out on Friday. Rinse and re­peat, every week.
He could bank episodes of *The Seen and the Unseen*, which now comes out fort­nightly. Not this one. “This was just on my mind all the time,” he said.
He did not want to stop. “Ajay and I both love the show,” he said. Only when the two talked and found they both had rea­sons did they agree to let it go.
~ Now, he said, it is time to take a pause, do some writ­ing and “get some chill back in my life”. {#chill}
stories.why: A fixed ca­dence is a prom­ise to the au­di­ence, and this one was kept for two and a half years. The cost, Varma found, was not the shoot­ing but the space it took in his head.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on never missing a Friday

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how this show escaped the ideas folder
stories.head: Fifty ideas in a folder
body: Amit Varma first tried to per­suade Ajay Shah to do a show to­gether three or four years ago, at a con­fer­ence in Udaipur. He for­gets ex­actly when. {128-S03}

He has dis­cussed many ideas with many peo­ple. In a cre­ative-ideas folder in Roam Research, he keeps some fifty YouTube ideas: a solo vlog, a show with this per­son or that. {#fifty} Most never hap­pen.

What made this one dif­fer­ent was that they sim­ply began. “We knew we would be im­per­fect at the start,” Varma said. “We knew that it would prob­a­bly be shit.” Some early mo­ments still make them cringe.
~ They started any­way, set the Friday ca­dence and stuck to it. Only through it­er­a­tion, Varma said, do you get bet­ter.

quote.text: But the dif­fer­ence is that you and I took ac­tion. We went into it, we said, let’s just start.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the folder of fifty ideas

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the intimacy of a new medium
stories.head: The viewer who butted in
body: Amit Varma once recorded an episode of *The Seen and the Unseen* with Abhinandan Sekhri. It is a story, he said, that he keeps going back to. {128-S04}
Someone who watched it later told Varma how it had felt: “I felt so much that I’m sit­ting with two friends and chat­ting in my liv­ing room that at one point I in­ter­rupted you.”
Varma loves the story for what it says about the medium. There was a time when stars were larger than life, he said. Today it is an in­ti­mate medium, “and that’s beau­ti­ful”.
~ That in­ti­macy, he ar­gued, is why being your­self works. It is easy, it is what peo­ple re­late to, and it is the only unique thing about you. {#beyourself}
stories.why: In an in­ti­mate medium the au­di­ence feels like a guest in the room, so a per­for­mance shows. Being your­self is the only thing that sets you apart from eight bil­lion oth­ers. {#billion}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the viewer who interrupted

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s advice to a friend starting a podcast
stories.head: Plan for the binge, not the debut
body: A few years ago, when *The Seen and the Unseen* was doing well, a dear friend of Amit Varma’s asked his ad­vice. She was about to start a pod­cast of her own. {128-S06}

His ad­vice was not to worry about how her au­di­ence would take the first episode. “Don’t think of what your au­di­ence will con­sume on episode one,” he told her. “Think of what they will binge at episode hun­dred.”
Her pod­cast, he said, went on to suc­ceed.

~ Worrying about light­ing, or about what your friends will say, gets in the way, Varma said. A show is a body of work: each weekly episode is flow, but to­gether they be­come a repos­i­tory. {128-C11}
stories.why: Judge a show by the cat­a­logue a new lis­tener can binge, not by the re­cep­tion of its first week. Weekly flow, kept up long enough, be­comes last­ing stock, which is how Varma sees this show’s ar­chive.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 128. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Robert Solow (Olaf Storbeck from Düsseldorf, Deutschland, CC BY-SA 2.0); Paul Graham (Sarah Harlin, public domain); Vijay Kelkar (Press Information Bureau, Government of India, GODL-India).

shelf.title: The Beauty of Finance (Episode 21)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on why fi­nance ex­ists and why it mat­ters to the real econ­omy: fi­nance as ‘the brain of the economy’, not a casino for the rich, traced back to me­dieval trad­ing voy­ages.

shelf.title: The episode on education
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Decades of both hosts’ think­ing on ed­u­ca­tion packed into about an hour, an episode Amit is proud of.

shelf.title: The episode on development economics
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The case, built on Lant Pritchett’s ev­i­dence, that every human wel­fare in­di­ca­tor tracks per capita GDP, so sus­tained growth, not re­dis­tri­bu­tion or small solv­able projects, is the way out of poverty.

shelf.title: Why Freedom Matters (early episode)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Despite the title, an eco­nomic his­tory of India told through the lens of free­dom: the boom after 1869, Nehru’s Fabian so­cial­ism, the lost years from the 1962 war to the Emergency, and the open­ing-up that lifted mil­lions out of poverty.

shelf.title: The Journey of Indian Finance series (incl. bankruptcy, inflation targeting)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: An insider’s ac­count of how Indian fi­nance was built: 25 years in which the fi­nance min­istry, SEBI, NSE and aca­demics worked to­gether, and how re­form pe­tered out once that group scat­tered.

shelf.title: Four Papers That Changed the World (Everything is Everything episode)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts ex­plain land­mark pa­pers in plain lan­guage, no­tably Coase on why firms exist and Hayek on how prices co­or­di­nate a so­ci­ety no plan­ner can grasp.

shelf.title: The episode on luxury beliefs
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: On be­liefs im­ported from rich-world dis­course that make their hold­ers feel vir­tu­ous while hurt­ing the peo­ple they claim to help, such as the min­i­mum wage, or op­pos­ing sweat­shops that beat every other op­tion work­ers have.

shelf.title: Life lessons from chess (second chess episode)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Lessons from chess on why re­newal mat­ters more than mas­tery (ex­perts in nar­row fields stop learn­ing), why young play­ers peak in a fi­nite game, and why a great firm re­cruits from all over the world.

shelf.title: Stories that should be films (episodes)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The first of the show’s se­ries of true sto­ries the hosts would turn into films, and Amit’s favourite episode at the time.

shelf.title: The episode on the creator economy
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Expands on the cre­ator lessons from the fi­nale: au­then­tic­ity, in­ti­macy, and the death of old gate­keep­ers.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: Forthcoming book on taxation
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar, Arvind Modi and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit is ‘fully con­vinced it’s gonna be great’, and it’s an­other piece of last­ing stock.

shelf.title: This Be the Verse
shelf.creator: Philip Larkin
shelf.why: A great poem whose image of sed­i­ment deep­en­ing like a coastal shelf Amit uses for how knowl­edge builds up in lay­ers across gen­er­a­tions, and can be washed away.

shelf.title: Ali Abdaal’s advice: don’t look at the numbers for two years
shelf.creator: Ali Abdaal
shelf.why: Ignoring early met­rics stops cre­ators from dumb­ing them­selves down to chase val­i­da­tion be­fore they have im­proved.

shelf.title: ‘Better to be loved by a few than liked by many’
shelf.creator: Paul Graham
shelf.why: Deep en­gage­ment builds trust, real com­mu­nity and bet­ter dis­course.

shelf.title: The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s long-form pod­cast of three-to-eight-hour deep dives, con­ver­sa­tions no gate­keeper would have com­mis­sioned, which have be­come an oral his­tory of India; its show notes list every book men­tioned.

laughs.text: Ajay says he has so many re­search pa­pers to write. Amit: ‘When you said so many, I was hop­ing you’re gonna say so many books’, a pub­lic nudge to write the books Amit keeps push­ing on him, like Invisible Infrastructure.
Amit, who cringes at his own footage, re­vives a line from his audio-only days: ‘I have a face for audio.’

Amit imag­ines pitch­ing the show to main­stream media: in­fla­tion tar­get­ing, the bank­ruptcy code, two hosts who ‘aren’t even like glam­orous, amaz­ing people’, and ‘nei­ther of us is a good-looking woman’. He quickly adds that Ajay’s ‘good looks and your shirts are legendary’.
Amit ad­mits every writ­ten piece of his has one typo that a reader flags within an hour. Spoken shows are no dif­fer­ent: ‘when we speak, there are al­ways typos, ver­bal typos will just hap­pen.’
‘No man steps in the same river twice’, the old line on con­stant flux, used in the show notes and by Amit as the frame for let­ting the show go.
